routes.description: Establish that classical theism offers a coherent and comparatively adequate explanation of central features of reality and withstands the principal objections raised against it.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if one or more independent theistic inferences remain reasonable under the relevant alternatives and suffering is not shown logically incompatible with classical theism.

motionBridge.description: Connect the surviving explanatory case and the coherence of classical theism to the intellectual reasonableness of personal theistic belief.

centralBridges.description: Show that the universe's contingent existence, beginning, or life-permitting conditions warrant a transcendent or intelligent explanation.
Show that intentional minds and objective moral obligations fit a personal divine foundation better than the proposed naturalistic account.
Show that omnipotence and perfect goodness can coexist with suffering when freedom and morally sufficient purposes constrain feasible worlds.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend explanatory power and other theoretical virtues as rational evidential standards alongside novel prediction.
Support a specifically historical inference to divine action from the evidence offered concerning Jesus's resurrection.

routes.description: Establish that the proposed theistic explanations lack sufficient evidential or conceptual support and that classical divine attributes conflict with the observed extent of suffering.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the central theistic inferences have viable naturalistic alternatives or defective premises and classical theism cannot coherently account for severe suffering.

motionBridge.description: Connect the evidential shortcomings and the unresolved problem of suffering to the conclusion that belief in classical theism is not intellectually reasonable.

centralBridges.description: Provide naturalistic causal or evolutionary alternatives that block the claimed necessity of divine explanations.
Show that invoking God lacks predictive or informative explanatory content sufficient to support the proposed inferences.
Show that an omnipotent and wholly benevolent God is incompatible with severe suffering absent a coherent necessity or greater-good account.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Challenge whether ancient testimony can discriminate resurrection from unreliable or analogous miracle claims.
Challenge divine-command and divine-nature accounts as foundations for objective moral standards.

sectionSelections.title: Cosmic Origin and Causal Explanation
sectionSelections.rationale: The need for an explanation of the universe and the status of quantum counterexamples determine whether a central inference to a transcendent personal cause can proceed.

proSelections.proposition: A contingent universe with a finite beginning is best explained by a transcendent, immaterial, personal creator.
Quantum-vacuum events do not establish emergence from nothing, and their causelessness remains disputed, so they do not defeat a causal inference from an absolute cosmic beginning.

conSelections.proposition: Pervasive quantum indeterminacy supplies events without sufficient causes and therefore challenges the causal principle used in cosmological arguments.
Uncaused alpha decay and quantum symmetry breaking undermine the assumption that the universe's earliest state must have a sufficient cause.

sectionSelections.title: Fine-Tuning and Explanatory Standards
sectionSelections.rationale: The comparative treatment of design, chance, physical necessity, and predictive power governs whether cosmic fine-tuning provides rational support for theism.

proSelections.proposition: The universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is better explained by design than by physical necessity or chance.
Predictive novelty is not the sole test of a hypothesis because explanatory power, simplicity, plausibility, and other theoretical virtues can also support theism.

conSelections.proposition: God lacks the predictive contribution that warrants accepting theoretical entities in science and therefore does not qualify as a reasonable scientific hypothesis.

sectionSelections.title: Intentionality and Scientific Naturalism
sectionSelections.rationale: Whether naturalism can coherently account for intentional thought and whether science entails the disputed philosophical consequences bears on the comparative reasonableness of the two worldviews.

proSelections.proposition: The evident existence of intentional mental states conflicts with materialist atheism's denial of aboutness while fitting a worldview grounded in a divine mind.
Metaphysical naturalism conflicts with reason and experience by denying intentionality, meaning, freedom, persistence, and persons.

conSelections.proposition: Atheism and the disputed philosophical doctrines are parallel implications attributed to science, so rejecting those doctrines does not logically refute atheism.
Denying intrinsic meaning and intentionality is not self-refuting because sounds, marks, and pixels can transmit information by causally reorganizing neural circuits.

sectionSelections.title: Objective Morality and Divine Grounding
sectionSelections.rationale: The debate over whether objective value and obligation require God supplies an independent route to theism and a central naturalistic challenge to that route.

proSelections.proposition: Objective moral values and duties exist, with values grounded in God and duties grounded in divine commands.
Moral values are grounded non-arbitrarily in God's essentially good character, while duties arise through commands that express that character.

conSelections.proposition: The Euthyphro dilemma and alternative ethical theories challenge the claim that objective morality depends on or uniquely indicates God.
Cross-cultural norms of fairness, equality, reciprocity, and cooperation can arise through natural selection because they enhanced human survival.

sectionSelections.title: Resurrection and Testimonial Evidence
sectionSelections.rationale: The reliability and comparative force of the offered historical evidence determine whether the specifically Christian resurrection inference contributes to the case for God.

proSelections.proposition: The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples' transformed belief are best explained by Jesus's resurrection, which entails God's existence.

conSelections.proposition: Ancient resurrection testimony is insufficiently reliable to justify a divine miracle, especially when comparable testimony for other religious claims is rejected.

sectionSelections.title: Divine Goodness, Freedom, and Suffering
sectionSelections.rationale: The compatibility of extensive human and animal suffering with omnipotence and perfect goodness directly controls whether classical theism remains coherent and reasonable.

proSelections.proposition: The logical problem of evil requires excluding the possibility that God has morally sufficient reasons for permitting suffering.
Creaturely freedom limits which worlds God can actualize, and humans cannot establish that comparable goods, salvation, and knowledge of God were feasible with less evil.

conSelections.proposition: Extensive suffering is logically incompatible with an omnipotent and benevolent God because such a being would eliminate suffering.
Freedom does not require catastrophic wrongdoing because God could create free agents who always choose rightly or never face suffering-producing circumstances.
